slides.punch: Four things in the filing. None made the press release.
slides.why: Revenue grew +28% this quarter and the stock barely moved. That headline is true and it is not the story. These four things are in the document behind it, not in the release, and we are going to take each one properly.
slides.notes: Meta just posted twenty-eight percent revenue growth and the stock barely moved on it. That headline is true and it is not the story. I read the ten-Q behind it, and here are four things that are in the filing and not in the press release. Each one changes how you should read this quarter, and we're going to take them one at a time.

slides.kicker: Start with the headline they sold
slides.head: Revenue up. Profit down. Cash gone.
slides.punch: Free cash flow: $784M, not a typo.
slides.why: Read the headline and you would expect this stock up. Operating income fell 8%, margin went from 43% to 31%, and free cash flow — cash left over after the business runs itself — nearly vanished. That gap between the top line and everything below it is the whole episode.
slides.notes: First, the quarter as they reported it. Revenue sixty point eight billion, up twenty-eight percent — genuinely strong. But operating income actually fell, margin went from forty-three percent to thirty-one, and free cash flow — the cash left over after the business runs itself — nearly vanished. That gap between the top line and everything below it is the whole episode.

slides.kicker: Why the earnings number is hard to trust
slides.head: Ten dollars of EPS, two one-time items
slides.sub: Reported diluted EPS against what it would have been without the item.
slides.why: A $15.9B one-time non-cash charge crushed Q3 2025 EPS to $1.05 — it would have been $7.25 without it. Two quarters later an $8.0B one-time benefit did the opposite, pushing EPS to $10.44. Same underlying business, $9.39 of reported EPS apart. Neither swing was really about the business.
slides.notes: Here's why the earnings number is so hard to trust right now. Third quarter last year, a fifteen point nine billion dollar one-time tax charge crushed EPS down to a dollar oh five — it would have been seven twenty-five without it. Two quarters later, an eight billion dollar one-time tax benefit did the opposite, pushing EPS up to ten forty-four. Same company, same underlying business, ten dollars of reported earnings per share apart. Neither number was really about the business.

slides.kicker: And that's not the end of it
slides.head: The IRS wants $15.9B more
slides.quote: In September 2025, we received a Statutory Notice of Deficiency ("2017-2019 Notice") from the IRS, asserting an additional $15.89 billion in tax, plus interest and penalties for our 2017 through 2019 tax years... The largest issue in the 2017-2019 Notice relates to the same underlying transfer pricing transaction that we litigated in the 2010 tax year trial and for which we received a Tax Court opinion in May 2025.

slides.punch: Built on a fight Meta already lost once.
slides.why: This is the company's own note, word for word. The IRS is asking for $15.9B more for 2017 through 2019, on the same transfer-pricing question a Tax Court already ruled on in May 2025 — valuing the intellectual property $1.5B higher than Meta had reported. This is not hypothetical risk language. It is a number, on an argument they have already partially lost.
slides.notes: And that's not the end of it — it's the preview. Buried in the tax note: the IRS is now asking for another fifteen point nine billion dollars for 2017 through 2019, on the exact transfer-pricing argument Meta already fought and partially lost in Tax Court last year. This isn't hypothetical risk language. It's a number, on a fight they've already lost once.

slides.kicker: Now the segment that actually earns it
slides.head: Revenue up. Family of Apps profit down.
slides.sub: Year-over-year change, Q2 2025 to Q2 2026 — same scale, both rows.
slides.why: Family of Apps — the ads business, the thing that funds everything else — grew revenue 28%. Its own operating income fell 6%. Why: the segment's own ‘other costs and expenses’ line — infrastructure, legal-related costs, partner arrangements — grew 75%, absorbing the legal charge and a share of the AI buildout. The business everyone thinks they are buying got less profitable this quarter, not more.
slides.notes: Now the finding that matters most for what this company is actually worth. Family of Apps — the ads business, the thing that pays for everything else — grew revenue nicely. Its operating income went the other way. Look at the two bars: revenue climbing, profit falling, same segment, same quarter. Legal costs and infrastructure spend landed inside the one business that is supposed to be the cash machine.

slides.kicker: Why infrastructure is eating the profit
slides.head: Capex guidance: raised. Never cut.
slides.sub: Full-year capex range at each release; FY26 is still guidance.
slides.why: Every release raised that range, and the final number still came in above the top of it. FY2026 started even higher, and it has already been raised again. This is not a company trimming its ambitions. It is why infrastructure costs keep outrunning the ad business underneath them.
slides.notes: Why is infrastructure eating the profit engine? Because the capital spending plan for this year has been revised upward at every single release — never once cut, never once held flat. It started the year at a range topping out around a hundred thirty-five billion and now sits even higher. This is not a company trimming its ambitions.

slides.kicker: And here's how it gets financed
slides.head: Two bond sales dwarf the rest
slides.sub: Every tranche of Meta's outstanding notes, by issue date.

legend.t: issued in the last nine months

slides.why: $55.0B of bonds in two sales, six months apart — more than the $29.0B Meta had issued in the three years it had carried any bond debt at all before that. Interest expense on the notes alone went from $232M to $754M in a single quarter, year over year. The AI buildout is being financed, not funded out of cash flow.
slides.notes: And here's how that spending actually gets paid for. Two bond sales, six months apart, twenty-five billion dollars or more each — bigger, combined, than every dollar of debt Meta had issued in its entire history before that. The interest bill on those bonds more than tripled year over year in a single quarter. The AI buildout is being financed, not just funded out of cash flow.

slides.punch: The buildout is bigger than today's balance sheet shows.
slides.why: In July, Meta agreed to hand a data-center campus to a joint venture for a 20% stake and a quick $1.0B payout — while guaranteeing up to $13.0B if the venture falls short. Add $279B of leases that have not even started and $349B of non-cancelable commitments sitting in the footnotes, and there is a lot more building than the balance sheet shows today.
slides.notes: And some of it isn't even on the balance sheet yet. In July, Meta agreed to hand a data center over to a joint venture for a twenty percent stake and a quick billion-dollar payout — while guaranteeing up to thirteen billion dollars if that venture falls short. Add in the leases that haven't even started and the non-cancelable commitments sitting in the footnotes, and there's a lot more building than the balance sheet shows today.

To be fair, 65% of those sales were set up months ahead on an automatic schedule, so do not read too much timing into it. But zero purchases, at any price, from anyone, is still zero.

To be fair, almost all of it runs through pre-scheduled trading plans set up months in advance, so don't read too much timing into it. But zero purchases, at any price, from anyone, is still zero.

The professionals are optimistic on the target and getting quietly less optimistic on the earnings that are supposed to get it there.

working: Advertising is still compounding — revenue up 28% with ad pricing and ad volume both growing double digits.
Family of Apps still produced $23.4B of operating income in the quarter, even after absorbing the legal charge.
The balance sheet still holds $90.3B of cash and marketable securities against $84.0B of bonds outstanding.
The Street models real upside: a mean target of $752M, and most covering analysts still rate it a buy.
Insider selling is real but modest and mostly scheduled — $374M against zero bought, 65% of it under pre-set 10b5-1 plans.
watch: Free cash flow is not a rounding error from zero — it already got there: $784M this quarter, down from $8.5B a year ago.
The IRS wants $15.9B more, on the same transfer-pricing argument Meta already lost the valuation fight over once.
$349B of contractual commitments and $279B of leases that have not even started yet sit outside today's balance sheet.
The El Paso joint venture guarantees up to $13.0B of residual value on assets Meta just moved off its own books for a 20% stake.
Buybacks are effectively paused while capex guidance keeps rising — free cash flow now decides whether the dividend and the new debt both keep getting paid.
why: The ad business is genuinely strong. Revenue grew 28% and both ad pricing and ad volume grew double digits — growth is not the question here.

But the profit and the cash did not follow it. Operating income fell 8%, free cash flow collapsed 91% to $784M, and Family of Apps — the segment that actually earns the money — saw its own operating income shrink 6%.
The balance sheet is doing a lot of the work. Meta raised $55B of new bonds in nine months and is now guaranteeing up to $13B on a data-center joint venture it just moved off its own books.

The tax line is not settled. Two one-time items swung diluted EPS from $1.05 to $10.44 in two quarters, and a live IRS notice puts another $15.89B on the table — on a transfer-pricing argument Meta already lost once in Tax Court.

The price is not the argument against this stock. At $589.85 you are already just below my base case of $612.81, and well below the $1,043.75 the AI bull case would require. What I am watching is not the tape — it is whether the tax dispute, the debt-funded buildout and the shrinking segment margin resolve.
